abstract: Background: Topographic maps organize the mammalian cortex, and their maladaptive reorganization underlies conditions like chronic tinnitus and focal dystonia. Low-intensity focused ultrasound (FUS) produces offline neuromodulation, yet its submillimeter spatial distribution within sensory maps remains poorly understood. Objective: To determine how offline FUS-induced amplitude changes are spatially organized within the mouse primary auditory cortex (A1) tonotopic map and depend on sonication intensity. Methods: Widefield Ca2+ imaging was combined with phased-array FUS (750 kHz, <1.5 W/cm2 Isppa, no microbubbles) in Thy1-GCaMP6s x CBA/CaJ mice. Twenty-second sonication was steered to each animal's tone-evoked centroid at 0.625 or 1.2 W/cm2. Offline gain was quantified over 40 min using Euclidean distance from the focus and functional distance (first principal component, PC1, percentile brackets). Results: Modulation followed functional rather than physical geometry: effects appeared isotropic in Euclidean distance but varied spatially across functional brackets, peaking 10 min post-sonication and persisting upwards of 40 min. Both intensities carved a modulatory trough between the 50th and 70th percentiles of A1's sensory representation (~1.0-1.2 mm from target). At 0.625 W/cm2 Isppa, this trough became suppressive (gain < 1.0) and shifted relative response timing across cortical fields, an effect absent at 1.2 W/cm2. Conclusions: Offline FUS modulation in A1 is organized by functional topography rather than physical distance, demonstrating that low-intensity FUS can serve as a spatially constrained suppressant. A forward-projection model built on this profile provides a quantitative basis for personalized, coordinate-based sonication planning for focal sensory pathologies like tinnitus.
